lesson.title: Why AI chatbots sometimes make things up
body: AI chatbots don't look facts up by default. They predict the most likely next words based on patterns in their training data. Most of the time that produces a sensible answer, but sometimes it produces something that sounds right and isn't.
These confident mistakes are called 'hallucinations'. They are most common with specific details: dates, figures, quotes, names, links and references to sources.

Tools that search the web or read your documents first reduce the problem, because the answer is based on text they've just read. They don't remove it: the tool can still misread or misquote the source.
lesson.takeaway: Use AI for drafts and ideas, but check any figure, date, quote or link against the original source before you rely on it.

m365.title: Pin your most-used chats to the top in Teams
m365.what: Pinned chats stay at the top of your chat list, so the people and groups you message most are always one click away.
try: Open Microsoft Teams and select Chat.
Hover over a chat you use often and select More options (…).
Select Pin. The chat moves to the Pinned section at the top of the list.
Repeat for other key chats. To remove one, select More options (…) again and choose Unpin.

explainer.story: Microsoft's 'Code Red' after its 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage
bullets: On 12–13 November a roughly 24-hour outage hit Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Microsoft 365 Copilot worldwide, disrupting governments, trading firms and airlines.

Microsoft said it was not a cyberattack. Reported causes differ: a network capacity change (BleepingComputer) or a Windows scalability defect introduced in July (Newsweek, citing internal memos). Satya Nadella apologised.

Internal 'Code Red' memos reported by Reuters freeze unrelated engineering work. Plans include load shedding, splitting traffic by region and faster recovery, with a goal of fixing worldwide incidents within an hour.
explainer.why: Many businesses run email, chat and files on Microsoft 365. How quickly Microsoft can contain the next failure matters to anyone who depends on it at work.

term.meaning: Deliberately turning away or delaying some work when a system is overloaded, so the most important services keep running instead of everything failing at once.
term.example: Microsoft's post-outage plan includes load shedding, so a surge in demand slows some features rather than taking down Outlook and Teams worldwide.
